tips.title: Current and pd swap roles
tips.body: **Series** shares the **potential difference** and keeps the current the same. **Parallel** shares the **current** and keeps the pd the same. One sentence gives you all six rules, and you never have to recall them as two separate lists.

tips.title: Make the shares add back up
tips.body: In series the pds must add to the **supply pd**; in parallel the branch currents must add to the **total current**. One line at the end of every calculation, and it catches nearly every slip earlier in the working.

tips.title: Total, then current, then the component
tips.body: For any series question: add the resistances, divide the supply pd by that total to get the current, then use $V = IR$ on the one component you were asked about. Four steps, always the same order.

tips.title: Bigger resistance, bigger pd — but smaller current
tips.body: In **series** the same current flows, so the bigger resistance takes the bigger **pd**. In **parallel** the same pd applies, so the bigger resistance carries the **smaller current**. Opposite, for the same reason.

tips.title: You never have to calculate a parallel total
tips.body: The spec says so explicitly. Know it is **less than the smallest branch** and be able to explain **why** — another path means more current for the same pd. If you are deriving a formula, you have misread the question.

why.matters:
There are only two ways to join things up, and everything electrical in a house, a car or a phone is one, the other, or a mix. In **series** there is one path, so the current is the same everywhere and the supply's pd is shared out. In **parallel** there is a path per branch, so each gets the full pd and the currents add.

The six rules are one decision made at the wiring stage, and you can read it off any circuit by asking: does the charge have a choice?

examples.title: Why the car's lights and heater each work on their own
examples.body:
Everything in a car hangs off one 12 V battery, and every one of them is wired **in parallel** across it. Each gets the full 12 V, so the radio does not dim when the heater comes on, and one blown headlamp leaves the other lit.

The price is current. A headlamp of 2.4 Ω draws $12 \div 2.4 = 5$ A, the heater fan at 1.2 Ω draws 10 A, and the battery has to supply the sum: 20 A with both lamps and the fan on. That is why the cable from the battery is as thick as a finger while the wire to one lamp is not.

visual.alt: A parallel circuit on a twelve volt car battery with two headlamps of two point four ohms and a heater fan of one point two ohms, each with the full twelve volts across it and the currents of five, five and ten amps adding to twenty

examples.title: Why fairy lights get dimmer as you add more
examples.body:
Cheap fairy lights are wired **in series**: one loop through every lamp. Each lamp adds its resistance to the loop, and the supply has to push the current through all of them.

With three 2 Ω lamps on 12 V the loop is 6 Ω, the current 2 A, and each lamp gets 4 V. Join a second set of three on the end and the loop is 12 Ω, the current 1 A, and each lamp gets 2 V: every lamp, old and new, is dimmer. The supply's pd is shared, and more lamps means a smaller share each.

examples.title: One dead bulb, two different outcomes
examples.body:
Old strings of Christmas lights were wired in series so that 20 small bulbs could share the mains: $230 \div 20 = 11.5$ V each, which a small bulb can take. The catch is the series rule: one path, so one dead bulb breaks the loop and every bulb goes out, and you find the culprit by trying each in turn.

A house is wired the other way. Every light and socket is its own branch in parallel, with the full 230 V across it, so a bulb blowing in the kitchen leaves the landing lit. Series shares the pd; parallel shares nothing but the supply.

steps.title: Two ways to join components
steps.body:
There are **two ways** of joining electrical components: **in series** and **in parallel**. Some circuits include both.

- **In series**, the components are in a **single loop**, one after another. There is only one path for the charge.
- **In parallel**, the components are on **separate branches**, so the charge has a **choice of paths**.

The practical difference is worth seeing before the rules: if one component in a **series** circuit breaks, the loop is broken and **everything stops**. In a **parallel** circuit the other branches keep working, which is why the lights in a house are wired in parallel and why one bulb failing does not darken the room.

The rules for each follow from that single fact about paths, and are worth learning as a contrasting pair rather than as two lists.

steps.title: The rules for series circuits
steps.body:
For components connected **in series**:

- there is the **same current through each component**;
- the **total potential difference of the power supply is shared** between the components;
- the **total resistance of two components is the sum** of the resistance of each component.

$$R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$$

Each rule makes sense from the single path. The charge has nowhere else to go, so the **same current** passes through everything. Each component takes a share of the energy each coulomb carries, so the **pd is shared**. And each component is one more obstacle in the only path, so the **resistances add**.

**How the pd shares out.** Not equally, unless the resistances are equal. The **bigger resistance takes the bigger share** — because the same current through a bigger resistance means a bigger $V = IR$. In a 4 Ω and 8 Ω pair on a 12 V supply, the 8 Ω resistor takes 8 V and the 4 Ω takes 4 V.

**Why adding resistors in series increases the total resistance.** Each extra component adds another obstacle to the **one path** the charge must take, so the total opposition rises and the current falls.

steps.title: The rules for parallel circuits
steps.body:
For components connected **in parallel**:

- the **potential difference across each component is the same**;
- the **total current through the whole circuit is the sum** of the currents through the separate components;
- the **total resistance of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor**.

Again each rule follows from the shape. Every branch is connected **directly across the supply**, so each gets the **full supply pd**. The charge divides between the branches and rejoins, so the branch currents **add** to the total. And adding a branch gives the charge **another route**, so more current flows overall — which means the **total resistance has fallen**.

**Why adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance** is worth being able to say in words, because it is the part students find least obvious:

**Each new branch is an extra path, so more current flows for the same pd — and more current for the same pd means less resistance.**

Think of it as opening another checkout: the queue moves faster even though the new till is no faster than the old one.

**One thing you do not have to do.** The specification says students are **not required to calculate** the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel. You need to know it is **less than the smallest** branch and be able to explain why — but no formula is required.

steps.title: Series circuits for measurement and testing
steps.body:
The spec asks you to **explain the design and use of dc series circuits for measurement and testing purposes**, which is a fancy way of describing the circuits you use in the practicals.

**Why series for measuring current.** An ammeter must have the current it is measuring pass **through** it, so it goes **in series**. Putting it in series also means it reads the current through **that whole loop**, which by the first rule is the current through every component in it.

**Why a voltmeter goes across.** Potential difference is measured **between two points** — the difference in energy per coulomb between one side of a component and the other. So a voltmeter is connected **in parallel**, across the component.

**A testing circuit.** To measure a component's resistance you put the component and an **ammeter in series**, a **voltmeter across the component**, and vary the supply. Then $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ at each setting. A series circuit is right here because it makes the current through the component easy to know and control.

**Combinations in series and parallel** were part of required practical 3. Connecting two identical resistors in **series doubles** the total resistance and **halves** the current; connecting them in **parallel** gives a total **below either one**, so the current rises. Measuring both confirms the two rules.

steps.title: Going deeper: why the rules are opposite
steps.body:
The two sets of rules mirror each other, and seeing the mirror halves what there is to learn:

| | Series | Parallel |
|---|---|---|
| **Current** | the **same** through each | **shared** between branches |
| **Potential difference** | **shared** between components | the **same** across each |
| **Adding a component** | total resistance **rises** | total resistance **falls** |

Current and potential difference **swap roles**. If you remember that series shares the *pd* and parallel shares the *current*, the whole table follows.

**Which component gets the bigger share?** Also opposite, and also worth reasoning rather than recalling:

- In **series**, the same current passes through both, so $V = IR$ makes the **bigger resistance** take the **bigger pd**.
- In **parallel**, the same pd is across both, so $I = \frac{V}{R}$ makes the **smaller resistance** carry the **bigger current**.

**Explaining the parallel case in words.** This is the one that carries the marks, because it is genuinely counter-intuitive:

> Each resistor added in parallel provides **another path** for the charge. With more paths available, **more current flows** for the same potential difference. Since more current for the same pd means **less resistance**, the total resistance falls — and it must end up **below** the smallest branch, because that branch alone already carried its own current and the others add to it.

That last clause is the strongest form of the argument, and it explains the *less than the smallest* rule rather than just stating it.

**A check worth doing every time.** In a series calculation, the individual pds must **add to the supply pd**. In a parallel one, the branch currents must **add to the total current**. One line each, and they catch almost every slip.

**What is not required.** You do **not** have to calculate the total resistance of two resistors in parallel. If you find yourself deriving a formula for it, you have misread the question — it is asking you to compare, or to explain, not to compute.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Components are joined **in series** (one loop, one path) or **in parallel** (separate branches).
- **Series**: the **same current** through each; the supply pd is **shared**; the resistances **add**, $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$.
- **Parallel**: the **same pd** across each; the branch currents **add** to the total; the total resistance is **less than the smallest** branch.
- Current and pd **swap roles** between the two, which is the quickest way to hold all six rules.
- In **series** the **bigger resistance** takes the **bigger pd**; in **parallel** the **smaller resistance** carries the **bigger current**.
- **Adding in series raises** the total resistance: another obstacle in the one path.
- **Adding in parallel lowers** it: another path, so more current for the same pd.
- Series order of working: **total resistance → current → the component you were asked about**.
- **Check**: series pds add to the supply pd; parallel branch currents add to the total.
- **Ammeter in series**, **voltmeter across** — each follows from what it measures.
- You are **not required** to calculate the total resistance of two resistors in parallel.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply is connected to a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor in series. Calculate the total resistance, the current in the circuit, and the potential difference across each resistor. Show a check on your answer.
questions.solution: In a series circuit the resistances add, so the total resistance is four plus eight, which is twelve ohms. The current is found from the supply potential difference and the total resistance, using current equals potential difference divided by resistance. This gives twelve divided by twelve, which is one ampere. In a series circuit the current is the same through every component, so one ampere flows through both resistors. The potential difference across the four ohm resistor is found from potential difference equals current times resistance, giving one times four, which is four volts. Across the eight ohm resistor it is one times eight, which is eight volts. As a check, the two potential differences should add up to the supply potential difference, and four volts plus eight volts is twelve volts, which matches the supply. The eight ohm resistor takes the larger share because the same current passes through both, so the larger resistance has the larger potential difference across it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Total resistance.** In series they add:

$$R = 4 + 8 = 12\ \Omega$$

**Current.** Use the supply pd and the **total** resistance:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1 \text{ A}$$

This current is the **same through both** resistors — there is only one path.

**The potential differences.** Apply $V = IR$ to each resistor separately:

- across the 4 Ω: $V = 1 \times 4 = 4$ V
- across the 8 Ω: $V = 1 \times 8 = 8$ V

**The check.** The pds must share out the supply pd:

$$4 + 8 = 12 \text{ V} \quad \checkmark$$

And the result makes sense: the **8 Ω** resistor takes the **larger** share, because the same current through a larger resistance gives a larger $V = IR$.

The check is one line and it is a mark of its own — it is also the thing that would have caught a rearranging error three steps earlier.

questions.prompt: Explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases the total resistance, while adding resistors in parallel decreases it. Refer to the paths available to the charge and to the potential difference in each case.
questions.solution: In a series circuit there is only one path for the charge to follow, so every component the charge passes through is a further obstacle to its flow. Adding another resistor therefore adds to the total opposition, so the total resistance increases and the current falls for the same supply potential difference. In a parallel circuit each resistor is connected directly across the supply, so each branch has the full supply potential difference across it. Adding another resistor in parallel provides an additional path for the charge to take. Because the supply potential difference has not changed but there is now an extra route, more current flows out of the supply altogether. Since resistance is the potential difference divided by the current, more current for the same potential difference means the total resistance has decreased. The total resistance must in fact be smaller than the smallest individual resistor, because that resistor alone was already carrying its own current and the other branches add further current on top of it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**In series.** There is only **one path** for the charge. Every component in that path is a further **obstacle** to the flow, so adding one adds to the total opposition: the **total resistance increases** and the current falls for the same supply pd.

**In parallel.** Each resistor is connected **directly across the supply**, so every branch has the **full supply pd** across it.

Adding another resistor in parallel gives the charge **another path**. The supply pd has **not** changed, but there is now an extra route, so **more current** flows out of the supply altogether.

Since

$$R = \frac{V}{I}$$

more current for the **same** pd means the **total resistance has fallen**.

**Why it must be below the smallest branch.** That branch on its own was already carrying its own current; the other branches add **further** current on top. So the total current is larger than any single branch's, and the total resistance smaller than any single branch's.

That last paragraph is what separates an explanation from a restatement: it gives a reason for the *less than the smallest* rule rather than quoting it.

examTechnique.body:
Decide first whether the circuit is series or parallel, because every rule depends on it.

For a series calculation, work in the fixed order: total resistance, then current, then V = IR on the component named.

Finish by checking that the shares add back up: pds to the supply pd in series, branch currents to the total in parallel.

For a parallel circuit, remember each branch has the full supply pd, so you can work on one branch at a time.

When asked to explain why resistance rises or falls, talk about the paths available to the charge, and say that the supply pd has not changed.

Do not try to calculate the total resistance of two parallel resistors: the specification does not require it, and the question is asking for a comparison or an explanation instead.
examinerErrors: Sharing the potential difference between parallel branches, where each gets the full pd.
Using one resistor's value instead of the total when finding the current in a series circuit.
Forgetting that the current is the same through every component in series.
Saying the total resistance of a parallel pair lies between the two values.
Giving the larger current to the larger resistance in a parallel circuit.
Omitting the check that the series pds add to the supply pd.
Explaining the parallel case without saying that the supply pd is unchanged.
Attempting a parallel resistance calculation that is not required.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer says which arrangement it is before doing anything, and works series questions in the same four steps every time. It checks that the shares add back up without being asked, and treats that check as part of the answer rather than as rough work. Explaining the parallel case, it mentions that the supply pd has **not** changed — the step most answers omit, and the one that makes the argument work. It can say why the total must be below the smallest branch rather than quoting the rule. And it holds the six rules as one idea: current and potential difference swapping roles between the two arrangements.
